doc.title: Tom Scott interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 1, 2022 [interview 1 of 2]

title: No rivalry among studio saxophonists
summary: He describes Ernie Watts, Plas Johnson, Sanborn, Brecker and Grover Washington as friends, not competitors.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Was there competition, friendly or not, between the saxophone players especially because if any wind instrument is going to get a gig playing solos it’s probably going to be a saxophone. So you have Ernie Watts and Plas Johnson and people at that level. Did you run into these other players and sort of like, “So what have you been doing lately? Who did you play with?”

Not at all. It was not like that at all. No. No. No. Look we were a fraternity of very lucky musicians who managed to get into this very heady department of the music business. So we were thrilled to be there. I considered them fellow travelers, fellow musicians who I respected and admired. But you know also there were others at the time, in addition to Ernie and Plas, there was David Sanborn, there was Michael Brecker, there was Grover Washington. Now those guys pretty much — I’m sure there are other people I’m not mentioning but we were very prominently featured as saxophone soloists. And you know look, you can’t take a gig away from somebody. I mean producers and artists like who they like and they’re going to call them. And at the time of course, unlike today, there was plenty of work for everybody to, you know, to survive and flourish. So it didn’t feel like that competition. In fact they were my buddies, especially David and Michael and Grover became a dear friend. Just great guys you know. Look, we had so much in common, our love for the saxophone and music and jazz. So you know what are you going to do, pretend you don’t like somebody like that or you’re in competition with them? It wasn’t a competition that way.
